title: Stopping Distances
whatItIs: The distance your car travels from the moment you see a hazard until it stops: thinking distance plus braking distance.
keyFacts: Overall stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
The table is a general guide: a dry road, a car in good condition and an alert driver.
On faster roads and in tunnels, leave at least a two-second gap to the vehicle in front.
On wet roads, at least double that gap: stopping distances are at least double.
On icy roads, stopping distances can be up to ten times longer than on dry roads.

visual.caption: Typical stopping distances on a dry road

a.label: Thinking distance
points: Grows in step with your speed
Longer if you're tired, distracted or have been drinking

b.label: Braking distance
points: Grows much faster than your speed
Longer on wet or icy roads and with worn tyres

onTheTest.question: You're driving at 50 mph on a dry road. What is the typical overall stopping distance?
onTheTest.why: At 50 mph: 15 m thinking + 38 m braking = 53 m (175 feet).

onTheTest.question: The road is wet. How much space should you leave to the vehicle in front, compared with a dry road?
onTheTest.why: Stopping distances at least double in the wet, so the two-second gap becomes at least four seconds.

traps: Don't confuse braking distance with overall stopping distance: add the thinking distance.
The table is for good conditions. Wet roads, ice, worn tyres or a tired driver all make it longer.
Double the speed is far more than double the distance: 30 mph is 23 m, 60 mph is 73 m.
